---
title: "How chromatograms become compounds"
description: "An analytical guide from known peak shapes to blind PSF estimation, flexible single-sample deconvolution and coupled multisample analysis."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

At each scan, a GC/MS instrument records an ion-intensity pattern across mass
channels. A chromatogram contains overlapping contributions from compounds,
a varying background and measurement noise. Deconvolution separates those
contributions into an elution profile and mass spectrum for each compound.
Integration measures its abundance; spectral and retention-index matching then
help identify it.

GCMSprime brings these steps into one workflow. This article explains the
modeling choices in chromatographic terms. The companion
[identification article](identification-theory.html) explains alkane calibration
and library search.

## 1. Begin with a known peak shape

Suppose a very narrow injection of one compound produces a known response
shape. This **point spread function**, or PSF, describes the instrumental peak
associated with a sharp input. Put a copy at each possible elution position;
the columns of the resulting design matrix represent candidate peaks.

A compound's coefficient gives its contribution to each ion trace. Most
candidate positions should have coefficient zero. Selecting a compact set of
positions and fitting their amplitudes is sparse regression. Joint selection
across mass channels uses the whole spectrum to support a peak call.

\[
\text{expected signal}=
\text{shifted PSF shapes}\times\text{ion amplitudes}
+\text{background}.
\]

[L0glm](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0glm/articles/deconvolution.html)
fits this fixed-shape model efficiently with an automatic regularization preset.
Its grouped selection identifies common candidate positions across channels,
and relaxed refitting estimates amplitudes on that support. Sparse pulse-train
deconvolution follows the idea of
[de Rooi & Eilers (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2011.05.030).

## 2. Estimate an unknown or changing PSF

Usually the instrument's response is not known exactly. A calibration standard
with isolated peaks gives direct information about it. GCMSprime can also
learn from overlapping sample peaks by alternating:

1. Fit candidate peak locations and ion amplitudes using the current shape.
2. Fit a revised common shape using those estimated locations and amplitudes.
3. Refit the sample with that shape and retain the better completed model.

Normalization puts overall intensity in the amplitudes, and centroid alignment
sets the kernel's time origin. An alkane standard provides a useful starting
shape; blind sample refinement adapts it to the sample signal.

Peak width can change along a chromatogram. Estimating the PSF in overlapping
windows and smoothly joining those local shapes gives a time-varying design.
The default full-chromatogram workflow uses ten PSF anchors. Each candidate
peak gets the shape appropriate to its own retention region.

These methods are implemented in
[L0nmf's PSF estimator](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0nmf/articles/estimate-psf.html).
GCMSprime handles CDF import, the supplied alkane file and sensible scan/time
conventions around that estimator.

## 3. Let individual compounds have different shapes

A shared PSF describes the common instrumental response. Compound chemistry
and concentration can cause additional broadening, overload, long tails or
sharp acid-like profiles. Several nearby fixed-shape peaks may then describe
different pieces of the same compound.

Sparse log-concave nonnegative matrix factorization gives each compound its
own shape. A convenient representation is

\[
\mu_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^{K}H_{ir}S_{rj}+(BA)_{ij}+O_{ij}.
\]

Here \(H\) contains elution profiles, \(S\) contains mass spectra, and
\(BA\) is a smooth background. Each compound contributes its profile multiplied
by its ion intensities. All factors are nonnegative. The optional \(O\) is known
additive signal.

Profiles are constrained to be **log-concave**: their logarithms bend downwards.
This permits asymmetric, tailed and triangular profiles while keeping each
component a coherent single peak. The shape is estimated using the chosen
noise model on the original intensities. Logarithms parameterize the positive
profile during the constrained update.

The algorithm begins with sparse PSF-based components. Spectral similarity,
profile overlap and shape compatibility suggest which components can be joined.
Local likelihood fits then refine the proposed profile and spectrum with other
compounds held fixed. The full fit criterion decides whether to keep a join.

## 4. Select the number of compounds automatically

A good fit must explain the signal with a compact set of compounds. GCMSprime
uses the likelihood together with a penalty on component count. With the GIC
preset, stronger evidence is required for adding a component than for adjusting
an existing component's profile or spectrum.

The rank criterion includes the original number of ion channels in its scale.
It leaves smooth background coefficients and profile complexity unpenalized.
The final model can delete unsupported components, join compatible fragments,
or add peaks supported by residual evidence. Every accepted rank change is
checked on all original channels.

For speed, initialization can aggregate ion traces into at most 32
intensity-adjusted groups. Final spectra and likelihood checks return to every
original channel. This preserves low-abundance diagnostic ions in the outputs.
Native local updates work only on the scan windows affected by a proposal.

The [L0nmf mathematical article](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0nmf/articles/algorithm.html)
gives the precise objectives, rank-charge convention, shape constraints,
initialization, solvers and pseudocode. Its likelihood formulation connects to
[deviance matrix factorization](https://doi.org/10.1214/23-EJS2174) and
[generalized matrix factorization](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v23/20-1104.html).
Positive shape modeling is motivated by
[Eilers' unimodal smoothing](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.935).

## 5. Model background and measurement variation

A low-dimensional nonnegative spline basis describes the smoothly varying
baseline. Its coefficients are fitted conditionally on the compound signal.
Full chromatograms use enough knots to follow gradual drift, while a short
window can use a constant background. Calibration peak detection starts from
a lower-quantile background estimate.

Poisson variance grows with expected counts. Instrument-exported intensities
often have additional variation, so the default quasipoisson model estimates
a common variance-to-mean scale. Gaussian, NB1/NB2 and Gamma signal models
are also available. Gamma zeros can represent left-censored measurements below
a specified detection threshold.

Temporal differences estimate noise after suppressing slowly varying signal.
An optional lag-one working adjustment accounts for correlated scan noise in
the rank charge. The fitted mean and marginal noise model determine Pearson
residuals, which make the residual heatmaps easier to compare across strong
and weak ion channels.

## 6. Integrate and inspect each sample

With unit-sum profiles, spectral coefficients carry the component's discrete
integrated intensities. GCMSprime reports these totals and time-weighted areas,
alongside normalized spectra for comparison. Output tables retain sample names,
retention times, widths and compound IDs. Profiles and spectra follow temporal
order by default.

Trace plots place fitted compounds over background-corrected observed ion traces.
Heatmaps show observations, corrected observations, fitted signal and Pearson
residuals. These views complement the profile/spectrum panels: they reveal where
the fit explains a broad peak, resolves neighbours or leaves residual structure.

The [single-sample tutorial](gcms-deconvolution.html) shows two experimental
windows, CDF export/import and the resulting MSP, Excel and PDF reports.

## 7. Analyze samples together

Across an experiment, retention times drift and a compound may change width,
tailing and abundance. Some compounds occur in only a subset of samples.
Coupled factorization starts from independent fits, then estimates a shared
spectrum for matched occurrences while retaining each sample's own profile,
area and background.

High-confidence spectral matches supply alignment anchors. An anchor uses the
leading 1%-height crossing plus half the width of a small peak in that region;
this reduces tail-related timing shifts. A robust smooth monotone map captures
drift, with concentration-related anchor motion accounted for separately.

Candidate matches must agree in spectral shape and aligned timing. Their
profiles are compared in area order to check compatibility with a coherent
log-concave ridge across samples. Shared spectra are then refined using pooled
evidence from every occurrence. The joint criterion counts a shared spectrum
once and each detected occurrence's amplitude separately.

Alignment retains the measured scan grids. It adjusts profile coordinates and
bin widths with an area-preserving Jacobian. Known exposure can be supplied
when the measurement represents integrated counts. Unit exposure preserves
vendor intensity units by default.

Observations and factor checkpoints are stored per sample on disk. Coupled
updates read one sample at a time, with common spectra and compact matching
summaries in memory. Nearby-time comparisons avoid an all-occurrence pairwise
distance matrix. Samples keep their acquisition order and group labels; alkane
standards are selected by acquisition time. Missing occurrences remain `NA`.

See [multiple-sample deconvolution](multisample.html) for the directory workflow
and [L0nmf's coupled model](https://tomwenseleers.github.io/L0nmf/articles/algorithm.html#coupled-model)
for the full mathematical specification.

## 8. Identify the recovered compounds

Open and commercial spectral libraries can be imported and searched. GCMSprime
uses alkane-derived retention indices to filter compatible candidates, then
ranks their spectral match quality. Consensus IDs connect repeated occurrences
for a unique-compound summary across the experiment.

[Retention indices and spectral identification](identification-theory.html)
explains the diagnostic-ion alkane assignments, calibration, column classes,
spectral distances and ion weighting. The
[library-search tutorial](library-search.html) shows the calls and annotated exports.
